output:
**What I found:** Finance's proposal would cut the CI runner pool from 10 to 8 to remove what looks like idle capacity. I recommend refusing the cut and putting a stop to finance's work on it (the record calls this **Reject**). The 22% "idle" capacity is the headroom that keeps queues short. The job count stays the same, so the same 7.8 runners' worth of work would fall on 8 runners. Utilization would go from 78% to 97.5%. The Kingman wait factor ρ/(1−ρ) would go from about 3.5 to 39, roughly 11 times worse, and peak load would likely be more than 8 runners can handle.

**Why it matters:** At about 11 times the queueing pressure, the average 9-minute wait could approach 1.5 hours. The 14:00–17:00 merge window already waits 31 minutes, more than the 12-minute job time. With 8 runners it would likely build a backlog that never drains during the window. If the cut is refused, nothing gets worse. The cost question then moves to the peak, which is uneven demand, not too many runners.

**Do this first:**
1. Pull per-hour runner utilization and queue depth for the last 30 days from the CI scheduler metrics. This confirms the peak utilization the estimate above assumes.
2. If finance still wants savings, test a policy change before any capacity change: cap or level non-urgent jobs in the 14:00–17:00 window, and check whether those jobs can be skipped or made cheaper.

**What I did not check:** I don't have the per-hour utilization data. The 97.5% figure and the peak backlog come from the 30-day averages. The command that closes this gap depends on your CI system's metrics API. I also didn't check how much job length varies, which Kingman also depends on. Your per-job duration export would close that.

Cut the pool: no

On the fallback: it fails the skill's litmus test. That test says a change that worsens any complexity axis (D diversity, K coupling, P depth, n quantity) without a measured gain in flow, reliability or cost is not an optimization. The split adds two lanes (D), a routing table that ties each repository to a lane (K), and a table entry for every repository (n). Nobody has measured what it does to queue time, so there is no gain to set against that. Queueing theory also predicts it makes waits worse: two separate pools can't lend idle runners to each other, so a busy lane queues while the other has free runners.

Litmus test: fail

```
Scope:          Shared CI runner pool, last 30 days
Constraint:     Runner pool during 14:00–17:00 merge window (wait 31 min > 12 min cycle time); hourly utilization Not measured
Decision:       Reject (cut to 8); Reject (3/7 split, fails litmus test)
Flow signal:    Utilization 78% avg → 97.5% at 8 runners; Kingman factor 3.5 → 39 (~11×); peak wait > cycle time = queued inventory; variation class: Mura (bursty merge arrivals), common cause
Evidence:       User-supplied 30-day metrics: 12 min avg job, 9 min avg wait, 31 min peak wait, steady daily job count
Next action:    Export per-hour utilization and queue depth; trial leveling or removing peak-window non-urgent jobs before any capacity change
Verification:   Not run — no scheduler data access; figures derived from stated averages
Residual risk:  Peak utilization and job-length variance unknown; split could only pass with a measured queue-time improvement that outweighs added D/K/n
```
